title: Asian Flush Pills: What Works, What Hides It, and Sunset Reviewed
excerpt: Do Asian flush pills actually work? An honest look at Pepcid, Zyrtec, Sunset, NAC, and other products sold for Asian glow, what each one does, and why hiding the flush doesn't hide the risk.
metaDescription: Do Asian flush pills work? Pepcid, Zyrtec, Sunset, NAC, and DHM compared honestly, plus why hiding the red face doesn't lower the health risk.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most "Asian flush pills" fall into two groups. The first is antihistamines, mainly Pepcid (famotidine) and sometimes Zyrtec or Allegra, which can make your face less red. The second is branded supplements such as Sunset, which are sold as "flush support" but have little independent evidence behind them. Neither group fixes the cause. The redness of Asian glow comes from a build-up of **acetaldehyde**, a toxic chemical your body makes when it breaks down alcohol, and no pill on the shelf has been shown to clear it faster in people who flush. Hiding the red face while the acetaldehyde stays high is the main risk with every product on this page.

**The quick rules:** If you use a pill to reduce the flush, drink exactly as little as you would without it. Never use the "your face isn't red, so you're fine" signal as a reason to have another drink. Avoid sedating antihistamines like Benadryl with alcohol. Be wary of any product promising to "stop," "cure," or "eliminate" Asian flush. And if you flush, the single most protective thing you can do is drink less, because the flush is your body warning you about a chemical linked to cancer of the throat and esophagus.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using any pill to reduce flushing if** you take prescription medicines, have kidney or liver problems, are pregnant or breastfeeding, have a heart rhythm problem, or are using flush pills most times you drink. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** a reaction to alcohol includes swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, trouble breathing, spreading hives, fainting, or chest pain.

## What Causes Asian Glow, in Plain Words

When you drink, your liver breaks alcohol down in two steps:

1. **Alcohol becomes acetaldehyde.** An enzyme called alcohol dehydrogenase does this first step. Acetaldehyde is toxic. It widens blood vessels, speeds up the heart, and causes nausea.
2. **Acetaldehyde becomes acetate.** A second enzyme, **ALDH2** (aldehyde dehydrogenase 2), turns acetaldehyde into acetate, which is harmless and eventually leaves your body as water and carbon dioxide.

Many people of East Asian descent carry a gene variant (often written ALDH2*2) that makes the second enzyme work poorly. Carry one copy and the enzyme runs at a small fraction of normal speed. Carry two copies and it barely works at all. Either way, acetaldehyde piles up after even one drink, and the result is the classic reaction: a red or blotchy face, neck, and chest, a racing heart, warmth, headache, and sometimes nausea.

A widely cited 2009 paper by Brooks and colleagues in *PLoS Medicine* estimated that about 540 million people worldwide, roughly 8% of the global population, carry this enzyme deficiency, and that at least a third of people of East Asian descent show the flushing response. If you want the fuller background, our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) and our explainer on [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) go deeper on the genetics and the other causes of a red face.

### Where histamine fits in

Acetaldehyde also triggers the release of **histamine**, the same chemical behind allergy symptoms. Histamine widens the small blood vessels in your skin, which adds to the redness. That's the only reason antihistamines help at all: they block part of the histamine response in the skin. They don't touch the acetaldehyde, which is the actual cause.

## The Masking Problem: Why a Less-Red Face Can Be Worse

This is the most important section on the page, so it comes before any product.

Acetaldehyde is classed by the World Health Organization's cancer agency (IARC) as a cause of cancer when it comes from drinking alcohol. People with the ALDH2 variant are exposed to much more of it per drink than people with a normal enzyme. Research, including the Brooks paper above, links ALDH2 deficiency plus regular drinking to a much higher risk of **esophageal cancer** compared with drinkers who have the normal enzyme. The red face is a visible sign that your acetaldehyde level is high.

When a pill turns down the redness, three things stay the same:

- **Your acetaldehyde level.** It's just as high as it would have been.
- **Your cancer-related exposure.** It depends on how much you drink, not on how red you look.
- **Your other symptoms, mostly.** Many people still get the fast heartbeat and some nausea.

What changes is the feedback. Without the flush, people tend to feel more "normal," and many end up drinking more than they would have. Researchers who study the flushing response have specifically warned that antihistamines used to hide Asian flush may encourage heavier drinking in the very people most at risk. So the honest framing for any flush pill is this: it's a cosmetic tool for a specific event, not protection. If you use one, set a drink limit before you start and keep to it.

## The Main Types of Asian Flush Pills, Compared

| Type | Common examples | What it does | What it doesn't do |
|---|---|---|---|
| H2 antihistamine | Pepcid / famotidine | Reduces skin redness for many people | Doesn't lower acetaldehyde or cancer risk |
| H1 antihistamine (non-drowsy) | Zyrtec (cetirizine), Allegra (fexofenadine), Claritin (loratadine) | May reduce redness and itch, often used with Pepcid | Doesn't lower acetaldehyde; some can add drowsiness with alcohol |
| H1 antihistamine (sedating) | Benadryl (diphenhydramine) | Blocks histamine | Strongly adds to alcohol's sedation. Avoid with drinking |
| Branded "flush support" supplements | Sunset and similar products | Claims to support acetaldehyde breakdown | No strong independent trials in people who flush |
| Single-ingredient supplements | NAC, L-cysteine, glutathione, B vitamins | Antioxidant or nutrient support | No good evidence they reduce flushing |
| DHM | Japanese raisin tree extract | Studied for alcohol metabolism and hangovers | No good evidence it reduces Asian flush |
| Gut probiotic | ZBiotics | Breaks down acetaldehyde in the gut | Doesn't reach the acetaldehyde in your blood that causes the flush |

The sections below go through each group.

## Pepcid (Famotidine): The Most Common "Asian Flush Pill"

Pepcid AC is a heartburn medicine. Its active ingredient, famotidine, blocks **H2 histamine receptors**. There are H2 receptors in your stomach (which is why it reduces acid) and also in the walls of small blood vessels in your skin. Blocking them makes those vessels widen less in response to histamine, so many people flush less.

**Pros:**

- Widely available, inexpensive, and well studied as a heartburn medicine.
- Many users report a noticeably less red face.
- Famotidine doesn't meaningfully raise blood alcohol levels the way an older drug in the same class, cimetidine (Tagamet), has been reported to in some studies.

**Cons:**

- Doesn't lower acetaldehyde, so the health risk behind the flush is unchanged.
- Results vary. Some people see a big difference, others very little.
- Taking it every weekend means taking a medicine you don't need for its labeled purpose. Long-term regular use deserves a conversation with your doctor.
- People with kidney problems need lower famotidine doses, so they should ask a doctor first.

People usually take a standard over-the-counter dose some time before drinking, following the label and not doubling up. We cover dose, timing, safety, and the popular Reddit routine in detail in our guide to [Pepcid for Asian flush](/never-hungover/pepcid-for-asian-flush).

## Zyrtec, Allegra, and Claritin: H1 Antihistamines

The other half of the histamine response runs through **H1 receptors**. These are the receptors that classic allergy pills block. Some people take a non-drowsy H1 blocker alongside Pepcid, on the theory that blocking both receptor types reduces redness more than either one alone.

**Pros:**

- Easy to find and familiar to most people.
- The pairing of an H1 and an H2 blocker is a common approach for other histamine-driven flushing, so the idea isn't far-fetched.

**Cons:**

- There's limited direct research on this combination for alcohol flushing specifically.
- Even "non-drowsy" options can make some people sleepy, and cetirizine (Zyrtec) is the most likely of the three to do so. Alcohol adds to that.
- Like Pepcid, they do nothing for acetaldehyde.

**Avoid Benadryl (diphenhydramine) and other older, sedating antihistamines when drinking.** Both they and alcohol slow down your brain, and together they can cause heavy drowsiness, poor coordination, and slowed breathing in high amounts. Our article on [antihistamines for alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/antihistamines-for-alcohol-intolerance) explains which ones interact with alcohol and how.

## Sunset Alcohol Flush Support: An Honest Review

Sunset is the best-known brand sold specifically as an "Asian flush" pill, so it's the product most people mean when they search for one. Here is a fair look at it. We don't sell or link to Sunset, and nothing here is a paid review.

**What it is.** Sunset is a dietary supplement, not a drug. It's marketed to help with alcohol flushing by supporting the body's handling of acetaldehyde and its antioxidant defenses. Products in this category are usually built from ingredients such as amino acids (for example NAC or L-cysteine), glutathione, and B vitamins. Formulas can change over time, so read the current label for the exact ingredients and amounts before you buy.

**What the evidence looks like.** As far as we're aware, there are no large, independent, placebo-controlled trials showing that Sunset reduces flushing or lowers blood acetaldehyde in people with the ALDH2 variant. Most of the support comes from customer reviews and from research on individual ingredients, which usually wasn't done in people who flush. Customer reviews for flush products are hard to judge, because how red you get varies a lot from night to night depending on what you drank, how fast, and whether you ate.

**Pros:**

- Made for a specific problem, and the marketing is aimed at the right chemical (acetaldehyde) rather than just the redness.
- The kinds of ingredients used in this category are generally well tolerated at normal supplement doses.
- Some customers say they feel better on nights they take it.

**Cons:**

- No strong independent evidence that it works for flushing.
- More expensive per night than a generic famotidine tablet.
- Supplements in the US aren't checked by the FDA for effectiveness before sale, and label accuracy can vary between brands.
- The same masking risk applies. If a product makes you feel like you can drink more, the acetaldehyde exposure goes up, not down.

**Our verdict.** If you're curious, Sunset is unlikely to harm a healthy adult at the labeled dose, but treat it as an experiment, not protection. There is no good evidence that it fixes the enzyme problem, and you shouldn't drink any more on nights you take it. Check with a pharmacist if you take prescription medicines, since some supplement ingredients can interact with drugs.

## Other Supplements Sold for Asian Glow

Many products repackage the same handful of ingredients. Here's what each one is, and what the evidence actually says.

### NAC (N-acetylcysteine)

NAC is a building block for **glutathione**, one of the body's main antioxidants. In hospitals, high-dose IV NAC is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose. As a daily supplement, its link to alcohol is mostly theoretical: glutathione helps the body deal with reactive chemicals like acetaldehyde. There is no good evidence that taking NAC before drinking reduces Asian flush. It can cause stomach upset in some people, and anyone on medication should check with a doctor first.

### L-cysteine

L-cysteine is an amino acid that can bind acetaldehyde directly. Small studies from Finland have looked at slow-release L-cysteine for lowering acetaldehyde in the mouth and for hangover symptoms. These are interesting, but they weren't designed to test flushing in people with the ALDH2 variant, and they don't show that a pill can bring blood acetaldehyde down to normal in someone whose enzyme barely works.

### Glutathione

Glutathione is the antioxidant that NAC and L-cysteine help your body make. Taken by mouth, much of it may be broken down in the gut before it's absorbed, and there's no good evidence that a glutathione pill reduces flushing.

### B vitamins and the niacin warning

B vitamins appear in many flush formulas. They're needed for normal energy metabolism, and heavy drinkers can run low on several of them. There's no good evidence that extra B vitamins reduce Asian flush in someone who already eats a normal diet.

**One B vitamin needs a warning: niacin (vitamin B3).** Regular niacin causes its own flushing reaction, often a hot, red, itchy face. Adding it to alcohol can make you redder, not less red. If a product contains niacin as "nicotinic acid," be aware it can cause flushing on its own.

### DHM (dihydromyricetin)

DHM comes from the Japanese raisin tree and is one of the most studied hangover supplements. Some animal studies suggest DHM may affect the enzymes that process alcohol and acetaldehyde. Those findings haven't been confirmed in people with the ALDH2 variant, and there is no good evidence that DHM reduces Asian flush. We cover where it does fit near the end of this article.

## ZBiotics and Other "Acetaldehyde" Probiotics

ZBiotics is a probiotic drink made with bacteria engineered to produce an enzyme that breaks down acetaldehyde. It sounds like a perfect fit for Asian glow, but there's a catch: the bacteria work **in your gut**. The acetaldehyde behind the flush is mainly made in your liver and travels in your bloodstream, which the bacteria can't reach. So there is no good evidence it reduces flushing for people with the gene variant. Our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review) looks at what it does and doesn't do.

## Not a Pill, but Worth Knowing: Redness Creams

Two prescription creams made for rosacea, **brimonidine gel** and **oxymetazoline cream**, work by temporarily narrowing the small blood vessels in the face. Some people with Asian flush ask their doctor about them for special events. They can reduce the visible redness for several hours, but they have exactly the same limitation as antihistamines: they work on your skin and do nothing about acetaldehyde. Some users also report rebound redness when the effect wears off. These are prescription products, so this is a conversation for your doctor, not something to borrow from a friend.

## How to Shop for an Asian Flush Pill Without Getting Fooled

If you're comparing products, these checks will save you money and protect your health:

- **Ignore "cure" language.** Any product claiming to "eliminate," "cure," or "permanently stop" Asian flush is overclaiming. The cause is genetic, and no pill changes your genes.
- **Ask what it actually targets.** Redness (antihistamines, creams) and acetaldehyde (claimed by supplements) are different things. Most products only touch the first, and the evidence for the second is weak.
- **Look for the full ingredient list with amounts.** "Proprietary blends" that hide how much of each ingredient is inside make it impossible to compare products or check for interactions.
- **Look for third-party testing.** Seals from independent testing groups (such as USP or NSF) show that a supplement contains what the label says. They don't prove it works.
- **Check for niacin.** As above, it can make flushing worse.
- **Don't stack products.** Taking Pepcid, Zyrtec, a flush supplement, and a hangover supplement all at once multiplies the chance of side effects and interactions without any evidence of extra benefit.

## Who Should Avoid Flush Pills or Ask First

Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using antihistamines or flush supplements with alcohol if you:

- Take prescription medicines, especially sedatives, sleep aids, anxiety or depression medicines, opioids, or blood thinners.
- Have kidney disease (famotidine and cetirizine doses may need to be lower).
- Have liver disease or have been told your liver enzymes are high.
- Have a heart rhythm problem or take medicines that affect heart rhythm.
- Are pregnant, trying to become pregnant, or breastfeeding.
- Notice you're using a flush pill nearly every time you drink.

That last point isn't about judgment. It's a sign that the flush is showing up often, and that's exactly the situation where the long-term risk from acetaldehyde adds up.

## What Actually Reduces Asian Flush

The things that genuinely lower your acetaldehyde load aren't sold in a bottle. They're about how much and how fast you drink:

- **Drink less in total.** Less alcohol means less acetaldehyde. Nothing else comes close.
- **Drink slowly.** Spacing drinks out (for example, no more than one per hour) gives your weak enzyme more time to keep up.
- **Eat before and while drinking.** Food slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which can soften the peak.
- **Alternate with water.** It slows your pace and keeps you hydrated.
- **Choose lower-alcohol drinks.** A light beer or a spritzer contains less alcohol per glass than a strong cocktail or a shot.
- **Know your limit and say so.** Many people with Asian flush find that one or two drinks is their honest maximum, and it's perfectly fine to stop there or not drink at all.

Switching to a different type of alcohol doesn't help on its own. Beer, wine, and spirits all produce the same acetaldehyde. Red wine may make things slightly worse for some people because it contains its own histamine and other compounds.

If you're unsure whether you carry the variant, the pattern is usually obvious (flushing after one drink since you first started drinking), but genetic tests can confirm it. Our guide on [alcohol metabolism genetic testing](/never-hungover/alcohol-metabolism-genetic-testing-complete-personalized-health-guide-2025) explains what these tests can tell you. And our [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) guide covers the habits with the best evidence, which help flushers as much as anyone.

## When to See a Doctor

A predictable flush after a drink or two that fades over an hour or so is common and usually not an emergency. But some reactions need attention.

**Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if you or a friend notice:**

- Swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or throat
- Wheezing, chest tightness, or trouble breathing
- Hives spreading across the body
- Fainting, or a pounding heartbeat with chest pain
- Confusion, repeated vomiting, or someone who can't be woken up after drinking

**Book a regular appointment if:**

- You started flushing for the first time as an adult, or the reaction is getting stronger
- You flush with tiny amounts of alcohol and also get stomach pain, diarrhea, or hives
- You flush and have a family history of esophageal, throat, or stomach cancer
- You started a new medicine and then began reacting to alcohol (some medicines cause flushing with alcohol)
- You're using flush pills most times you drink

New or changing reactions can have other causes, from medicines to other health conditions. Our guide to [alcohol intolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-intolerance) walks through the possibilities. A doctor can also talk with you about whether earlier screening makes sense if you flush and drink regularly.

## Where DHM Fits In (and Where It Doesn't)

Because we write about DHM, readers often ask whether it's an Asian flush pill. It isn't, and we don't recommend it as one. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces flushing or fixes the ALDH2 enzyme problem, and it shouldn't be used as a reason to drink more if you flush.

Where people do use DHM is as part of a general hangover routine for social drinking. The human research is still limited, and most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, so think of it as promising rather than proven. If you'd like to try it for that purpose, two well-known options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers amounts and timing, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you flush, the drink limit you set for yourself matters far more than any supplement.

For the full picture of why the flush happens and what it means for your health, see our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive).

## The Bottom Line

- "Asian flush pills" are mostly antihistamines (Pepcid, sometimes with Zyrtec or Allegra) or branded supplements like Sunset.
- Antihistamines can reduce the redness for many people. They don't lower acetaldehyde, the toxic chemical behind the flush.
- Sunset and similar supplements lack strong independent evidence. They're unlikely to harm a healthy adult at label doses, but there is no good evidence they fix the enzyme problem.
- NAC, L-cysteine, glutathione, B vitamins, DHM, and gut probiotics like ZBiotics all lack good evidence for reducing Asian flush. Avoid products with niacin, which can cause flushing on its own.
- Hiding the flush doesn't hide the risk. If you use any of these, drink exactly as little as you would without it.
- Drinking less and drinking slower are the only approaches that reliably reduce your acetaldehyde exposure.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What pills work for Asian flush?**

The pills most people use are antihistamines. Pepcid (famotidine), an H2 blocker, reduces facial redness for many people, and some add a non-drowsy H1 blocker like Zyrtec or Allegra. Branded supplements such as Sunset are also sold for flushing, but they lack strong independent evidence. None of these lower acetaldehyde, the toxic chemical that causes the flush, so they change how you look, not the underlying risk.

**Does Sunset work for Asian flush?**

As far as we're aware, there are no large independent, placebo-controlled trials showing that Sunset reduces flushing or lowers blood acetaldehyde in people with the ALDH2 gene variant. Some customers report feeling better, and its typical ingredients are generally well tolerated at label doses, but there is no good evidence that it fixes the enzyme problem. If you try it, don't drink more on nights you take it, and check with a pharmacist if you take prescription medicines.

**Is it safe to take Pepcid to hide Asian flush?**

For most healthy adults, a standard over-the-counter dose of famotidine with moderate drinking has no known dangerous interaction. The bigger concern is masking: Pepcid hides the redness but doesn't lower acetaldehyde, which is linked to esophageal cancer in people who flush and drink regularly. If you use it, keep your drinking as light as you would without it, and talk to your doctor if you have kidney problems or find yourself using it most times you drink.

**Can you take Pepcid and Zyrtec together for Asian glow?**

Many people combine an H2 blocker (Pepcid) with a non-drowsy H1 blocker (Zyrtec or Allegra) to reduce redness, and the two are commonly used together for other histamine-related problems. Direct research on the combination for alcohol flushing is limited. Cetirizine can cause drowsiness that alcohol makes worse, and neither drug lowers acetaldehyde. Avoid sedating antihistamines like Benadryl when drinking, and ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

**Is there a pill that cures Asian flush?**

No. Asian flush is caused by a genetic variant that makes the ALDH2 enzyme work poorly, and no pill changes that. Antihistamines can reduce the redness and some supplements claim to support acetaldehyde breakdown, but there is no good evidence any product restores normal acetaldehyde clearance. Be skeptical of any product promising to cure or eliminate the flush. Drinking less and more slowly is the only reliable way to lower acetaldehyde exposure.

**Does DHM help with Asian flush?**

There is no good evidence that DHM reduces Asian flush or fixes the ALDH2 enzyme problem. Some animal studies suggest DHM may affect alcohol-processing enzymes, but this hasn't been shown in people with the gene variant. Some people use DHM as part of a general hangover routine, where the human evidence is still limited. It shouldn't be used as a reason to drink more if you flush.

**Why shouldn't you hide Asian flush?**

The flush is a visible sign that acetaldehyde, a chemical classed as a cause of cancer when it comes from alcohol, is building up in your body. Hiding the redness doesn't lower that chemical, and research links ALDH2 deficiency plus regular drinking to a much higher risk of esophageal cancer. Without the warning sign, many people drink more than they otherwise would, which raises their exposure further.

**Does ZBiotics stop Asian flush?**

There is no good evidence that it does. ZBiotics uses engineered bacteria that break down acetaldehyde in the gut, but the acetaldehyde behind the flush is mainly made in the liver and travels in the bloodstream, which the bacteria can't reach. People with the ALDH2 variant should not expect it to prevent flushing or lower their cancer-related risk.
